classification.classification_note: The fix adds an `obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN` guard around the PIN APIs in the fuzzer loop. Without that guard, a JPKI certificate object's 352-byte `sc_pkcs15_cert_info` buffer is misrouted into PIN validation and overread as `sc_pkcs15_auth_info`.

bug_description.original: The vulnerability allows the code to attempt to validate a PIN even when the input is not actually a PIN, due to missing checks in the validation logic. This occurs in the PIN validation process.
bug_description.normalized: The staged fake-reader transcript first seeds `reader->atr` with a 32-byte value that does not match the only hardcoded JPKI ATR. After `sc_connect_card()` copies that ATR into `card->atr`, `jpki_match_card()` falls through its `_sc_match_atr()` fast path and relies on `jpki_select_ap()`, whose APDU response bytes also come from later overlapping chunks of the same transcript, to set `card->type = SC_CARD_TYPE_JPKI_BASE`. `sc_pkcs15_bind()` then admits the synthetic JPKI PKCS#15 emulator, which appends four certificate objects before the two PIN objects and allocates each certificate object's `obj->data` as a 352-byte `struct sc_pkcs15_cert_info`. `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput()` iterates that list from the head and, missing an `obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN` guard, calls `sc_pkcs15_verify_pin()` on a certificate object. The verifier blindly casts the certificate buffer to `struct sc_pkcs15_auth_info *`. In the reproduced x86_64 build, that miscast makes `auth_info->auth_type` overlap `cert_info.path.aid.len`; certificate construction leaves that field zero, and `SC_PKCS15_PIN_AUTH_TYPE_PIN` is also zero, so `_validate_pin()` does not take its non-PIN early return. Its next read, `auth_info->attrs.pin.stored_length`, sits at offset 352 of `struct sc_pkcs15_auth_info`, exactly one `size_t` past the 352-byte certificate allocation, and AddressSanitizer reports the resulting 8-byte heap-buffer-overflow read. The fix wraps the PIN API calls in `if (obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN)`.

source.description: First project-side consumption of the witness that creates vulnerability-relevant state: the fake reader decodes the first transcript chunk and copies it into `reader->atr` for later card matching.
source.value_from: The staged `gt_results/arvo_18540/poc` file is a 170-byte fake-reader transcript. Under `fuzz_get_chunk()`'s 2-byte overlapping format, the first call uses size byte `0x20` and yields the 32 ATR bytes `20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 ff 20 ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20`.

sink.description: ASan sink. `_validate_pin()` reads `stored_length` from a miscast certificate buffer as though it were `struct sc_pkcs15_auth_info`, overrunning the 352-byte certificate allocation.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 8` at `src/libopensc/pkcs15-pin.c:270:27`, at address `0x6130000001a0`, which is exactly 0 bytes past the 352-byte region `[0x613000000040,0x6130000001a0)` allocated in `sc_pkcs15emu_object_add()`.

root_cause.description: The loop invokes the PIN verifier on every PKCS#15 object without first checking that the current object is a PIN object, so a certificate object reaches `sc_pkcs15_verify_pin()`.
root_cause.note: The fixing diff wraps `sc_pkcs15_verify_pin`, `sc_pkcs15_change_pin`, `sc_pkcs15_unblock_pin`, and `sc_pkcs15_get_pin_info` in `if (obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN) { ... }`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The libFuzzer input buffer is stored as the fake reader transcript. Every later `fuzz_get_chunk()` call, including the ATR copy, APDU responses, and later `in`/`param` buffers, reads from this saved `Data`/`Size` pair by advancing the pointer two bytes per call.

parser_admitted.description: The saved run reaches synthetic PKCS#15 binding far enough for `sc_pkcs15_bind()` to return a non-null `p15card`, so the object iteration and unguarded PIN API calls execute.

evidence_limitations: The saved artifacts do not preserve which `fuzz_reader_transmit()` call supplied the successful `jpki_select_ap()` response. That fallback success is inferred from the non-matching ATR at the scored source plus the saved ASan allocation stack reaching `sc_pkcs15emu_jpki_init()`.

The ASan allocation stack identifies the certificate-add call site at `pkcs15-jpki.c:92`, but it does not record which of the four JPKI certificate iterations became the crashing object. The same missing guard would misroute any of those certificate objects into PIN validation.

The `auth_type` and `stored_length` offset reasoning is derived from the staged vulnerable headers together with the reproduced x86_64 build shown in `vulnerable_compile.log`; Stage 02 did not add runtime instrumentation to measure those offsets.

coarse_trace.summary: The fake reader copies the first transcript chunk into `reader->atr`, creating the attacker-controlled ATR state later used for card matching.

The witness ATR does not match JPKI's hardcoded ATR, so JPKI recognition falls through to `jpki_select_ap()`, whose APDU response bytes come from later overlapping chunks of the same fake-reader transcript and make the driver set `card->type = SC_CARD_TYPE_JPKI_BASE`.
Synthetic JPKI binding is admitted by that card type and adds four certificate objects before the two PIN objects; each certificate object allocates a 352-byte `sc_pkcs15_cert_info` buffer.
The object loop starts at the head of the append-ordered list, so early iterations bind `obj` to a certificate object rather than to a PIN object.
Because the vulnerable loop lacks `obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN`, it calls `sc_pkcs15_verify_pin()` on that certificate object.

PIN validation miscasts the certificate buffer as `sc_pkcs15_auth_info`, the inner non-PIN check falls through on zeroed certificate-path bytes, and the next `stored_length` read overruns the 352-byte allocation.

fine_trace.note: The first `fuzz_get_chunk()` call consumes the witness through the saved `reader->drv_data` buffer, returns 32 bytes, and copies them into `reader->atr`. On the saved witness those ATR bytes are `20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 ff 20 ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20`.
Card setup copies the staged ATR from step 1 into `card->atr`, which is the value later passed to built-in driver matching and `_sc_match_atr()`.

During `sc_connect_card()`'s built-in driver loop, the JPKI driver compares `card->atr` from step 2 against the only hardcoded JPKI ATR `3b:e0:00:ff:81:31:fe:45:14`. The witness ATR from step 1 differs immediately, so `_sc_match_atr()` returns negative and this fast path does not identify the card.

Later `sc_select_file()` traffic reads more overlapping chunks from the same saved transcript and materializes them as APDU status/data. The exact successful transmit call is not logged, but `fuzz_reader_transmit()` is the only project code that can synthesize the `jpki_select_ap()` response bytes.

Because step 3 rejected the hardcoded ATR and the saved run later reaches `sc_pkcs15emu_jpki_init()`, the fallback `jpki_select_ap()` path must succeed on the witnessed APDU response from step 4. That writes `card->type = SC_CARD_TYPE_JPKI_BASE` and identifies the card as JPKI.

Synthetic JPKI emulation is gated on the exact card type written in step 5. With `card->type` equal to `SC_CARD_TYPE_JPKI_BASE`, `sc_pkcs15_bind()` can admit `sc_pkcs15emu_jpki_init()` instead of rejecting the card as `SC_ERROR_WRONG_CARD`.

JPKI initialization first executes the four-certificate loop before the later two-PIN loop. Each certificate record starts from all-zero `cert_info`; `sc_format_path()` also zeroes the whole `sc_path` and then fills only file-id members, so `cert_info.path.aid.len` remains 0 on these certificate objects.

Certificate-class dispatch fixes `obj->data` to a 352-byte `struct sc_pkcs15_cert_info` buffer and copies the zero-initialized certificate record from step 7 into it. The saved ASan allocation stack matches this `calloc` site exactly.

Each new PKCS#15 object is appended at the tail without reordering earlier nodes. Because step 7 completes the four certificate insertions before the PIN loop starts, the head and early entries of `p15card->obj_list` are certificate objects.

fine_trace.code: for (obj = p15card->obj_list; obj != NULL; obj = obj->next) {
fine_trace.note: The fuzzer loop starts from the list head built in step 9. On the admitted JPKI path, the first visited objects are certificates, not PIN objects.

Missing guard: the loop calls the PIN verifier on every object instead of first requiring `obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN`. The fix wraps this whole PIN-API block in that condition, but in the vulnerable code a certificate object from step 10 is passed into `sc_pkcs15_verify_pin()`.

The verifier blindly reinterprets `pin_obj->data` as `struct sc_pkcs15_auth_info *` with no object-type validation. For the certificate object from steps 7-11, this recasts the 352-byte certificate buffer from step 8 as PIN-auth metadata.

In the reproduced x86_64 build, `struct sc_pkcs15_auth_info.auth_type` is at offset 328. When the step-8 certificate buffer is miscast, that field overlaps `struct sc_pkcs15_cert_info.path.aid.len`; step 7 left `path.aid.len` at 0, and `SC_PKCS15_PIN_AUTH_TYPE_PIN` is also 0, so this non-PIN early-return check falls through instead of stopping the call.

In the same x86_64 layout, `stored_length` sits at offset 352 of `struct sc_pkcs15_auth_info`, so reading it from the miscast 352-byte certificate allocation touches the first 8 bytes beyond the buffer. AddressSanitizer reports exactly this 8-byte read at address `0x6130000001a0`, immediately after the allocation from step 8.

format.contract: The exact 170-byte witness is interpreted by `fuzz_get_chunk()` with 2-byte-overlap semantics. Its first chunk has size byte `0x20` and produces the 32 ATR bytes `20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 ff 20 ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20`, which do not match JPKI's hardcoded ATR; later overlapping chunks from the same transcript must still make `jpki_select_ap()` return `SC_SUCCESS` so `sc_pkcs15_bind()` chooses the synthetic JPKI profile. Under that admitted state, the object loop must reach `sc_pkcs15_verify_pin()` on a certificate object because the vulnerable loop lacks `obj->type == SC_PKCS15_TYPE_AUTH_PIN`. The later `in` and `param` bytes are not part of the witnessed memory-safety trigger because the crash happens before the PIN contents are semantically used.
